core: HIPAA = Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-191); Administrative Simplification (Title II) directed HHS to write implementing rules
The implementing rules are codified in 45 CFR Parts 160, 162, and 164
Part 164 Subpart E = Privacy Rule; Subpart C = Security Rule (administrative/physical/technical safeguards for ePHI); Subpart D = Breach Notification Rule
Part 162 = Transactions and Code Sets and unique identifiers (e.g., National Provider Identifier, employer identifier)
Part 160 = general provisions, definitions (covered entity, business associate), and enforcement/civil money penalties
Regulated parties are covered entities and business associates; business associate agreements (BAAs) are required
The HITECH Act (2009, within ARRA) strengthened enforcement, added breach notification, and made business associates directly liable; implemented by the 2013 Omnibus Rule
Enforcement by HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR); civil penalties are tiered by culpability and inflation-adjusted; criminal penalties under 42 U.S.C. 1320d-6
supporting: Title II sections 261-264 are the Administrative Simplification provisions
Security Rule general requirement: ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI (45 CFR 164.306)
Breach Notification timing: notify individuals without unreasonable delay, no later than 60 calendar days after discovery (45 CFR 164.404)
Civil penalty amounts adjusted annually under the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act and published at 45 CFR Part 102

claims.claim: HIPAA is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, Public Law 104-191, enacted August 21, 1996; its Title II Administrative Simplification provisions (sections 261-264) directed HHS to adopt national standards for electronic transactions, identifiers, privacy, and security.
The HIPAA Administrative Simplification rules are codified in 45 CFR Parts 160 (general administrative requirements), 162 (transactions, code sets, and identifiers), and 164 (security and privacy).

The Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart C) requires covered entities and business associates to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of electronic protected health information through administrative (164.308), physical (164.310), and technical (164.312) safeguards.

The Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart D) requires notice after a breach of unsecured PHI to affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery.

A covered entity is a health plan, a health care clearinghouse, or a health care provider who transmits health information electronically in connection with a covered transaction; a business associate is a person or organization that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI to perform a function on behalf of a covered entity (45 CFR 160.103), and a business associate agreement is required.

The HITECH Act, enacted within the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, strengthened HIPAA — creating the Breach Notification Rule, making business associates directly liable, and adopting a tiered civil money penalty structure — as implemented by the 2013 Omnibus Rule (78 FR 5566, effective March 26, 2013).

HHS's Office for Civil Rights enforces the HIPAA Rules; civil money penalties under 45 CFR Part 160, Subpart D scale across four culpability tiers (did not know; reasonable cause and not willful neglect; willful neglect corrected; willful neglect not corrected), with dollar amounts adjusted annually for inflation and published at 45 CFR Part 102.

Criminal penalties for knowing wrongful disclosure of individually identifiable health information (42 U.S.C. 1320d-6) escalate across three levels: a base offense (up to $50,000 and 1 year), offenses under false pretenses (up to $100,000 and 5 years), and offenses with intent to sell or use PHI for commercial advantage or personal gain (up to $250,000 and 10 years).

Part 162 contains the standard electronic transactions and code sets and the unique identifiers, including the National Provider Identifier (Subpart D) and the standard employer identifier (Subpart F).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact dollar amounts of HIPAA civil money penalties
positions: The regulation states statutory per-violation ranges (e.g., a floor around $100 and a maximum of $50,000 per violation) and an annual cap for identical violations
The same regulation states those amounts are adjusted for inflation each year and published at 45 CFR Part 102, so the operative numbers differ from the statutory baseline
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four-tier culpability structure and cites amounts as inflation-adjusted ("as adjusted," published at 45 CFR Part 102) rather than asserting a single fixed current figure, avoiding a stale number.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('HIPAA Foundations is a foundational concept... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no substantive legal content; none of it was usable and all was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual statutory-and-regulatory architecture verified against primary sources.
Specified the correct subpart mapping (Privacy = 164 Subpart E, Security = 164 Subpart C, Breach = 164 Subpart D, Transactions/Identifiers = Part 162, general/enforcement = Part 160).
Handled penalty amounts as inflation-adjusted tiers rather than fixed figures.
rightsIssues: All primary legal sources (eCFR, U.S. Code, Statutes at Large, Federal Register, CMS.gov) are U.S. government works in the public domain. No HHS OCR guidance text was reproduced; requirements are restated in original wording.
